extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific method, philosophy of science readers, and scientists interested in methodological fallacies
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying methodological principles and cautions about scientific reasoning—identifying a priori fallacies and correct empirical procedures in inquiry. Focuses on what to avoid (common prejudices/fallacies) and what to prefer (experience and correct experimental approaches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reification of general terms / Mysticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating general terms (names of qualities or species) as denoting distinct objective entities (Universal Substances); e.g., taking 'whiteness' or 'man in general' to be real beings distinct from individual things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that supposing general language to name real, immutable substances (Substantiæ Secundæ, τὸ ὄν, τὸ ἔν) destroys intelligible discussion and leads to 'Mysticism'—ascribing objective existence to subjective creations. Example: regarding 'whiteness' as an entity inhering in white substances. Anti-pattern: believing that because we can speak of 'man' in general, there must be an abstract universal man distinct from individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid imputing nature's incapacities from our intellectual incapacities
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not conclude that because we cannot conceive a thing, nature cannot do it; do not assume nature is limited by our powers of conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prejudice leads to asserting that nature cannot perform what we cannot mentally conceive. Example: arguing from inability to conceive to impossibility in nature is a fallacy. Related misuse: using our lack of reasons to suppose a phenomenon must adhere to a particular law (see Principle of Sufficient Reason misuse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Misuse of the Principle of Sufficient Reason (inferring laws a priori)
rubrics_metrics.description: Asserting that a phenomenon must follow a certain law because we see no reason why it should deviate from that law (e.g., deducing inertia because there is 'no reason' for motion to be in one direction rather than another).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage calls such reasoning 'entirely fallacious' and illustrates with the law of inertia and the first law of motion: arguing that a body at rest cannot begin to move because there is no reason it should move one way rather than another is circular. Anti-pattern: proving physical laws 'a priori' by eliminating alternatives based on absence of a reason rather than by experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical confirmation over a priori proof for physical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The real and only proof of laws of the universe is experience; a priori demonstrations in physics are unreliable and often untenable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although mathematicians (e.g., Archimedes) and geometers sometimes prefer 'a priori' demonstrations, for empirical physical laws one must rely on observation and experiment. Example: the text stresses that laws of motion should be established by experience because only experience can show whether there are reasons for deviations. Anti-pattern: favoring purely deductive, non-experimental reasoning to establish empirical laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language-based fallacy: assuming linguistic distinctions map to natural distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that the differences in popular/common language and the classes it creates correspond to real, distinct differences in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Greek philosophers' mistake: taking the relations and distinctions present in common language (the ways we say something is 'in' something else, or the labels we use) as foundations for natural philosophy. Example: thinking that by determining the meaning of words one can become acquainted with facts. Anti-pattern: letting the accidental structure of a language dictate the classification and presumed natural divisions of phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Contrarieties (deriving natural oppositions from linguistic contrasts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that adjectival or conceptual oppositions found in language point to fundamental antitheses in nature (e.g., deriving metaphysical principles from contrasts like One/Many, Rest/Motion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cites Pythagorean and Aristotelian examples: collecting principles from contrasts suggested by number and deducing doctrines (like four elements) from oppositions. Anti-pattern: inferring deep natural laws simply because language presents paired opposites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assuming a single invariant cause (Bacon's oversight of plurality of causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject the tacit assumption that a phenomenon has one single, universal 'forma' or cause; many phenomena depend on a variety of distinct causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon's method of seeking one invariable condition for, say, heat, is criticized as assuming unity of cause where none exists—especially for sensible qualities. Guidance: recognize and allow for plurality of causes; do not restrict inquiry to searching for a single necessary cause. Anti-pattern: using negative instances to eliminate everything except one supposed 'form' and assuming that must be the cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological preference: study effects of a given cause rather than causes of a given effect
rubrics_metrics.description: It is generally more fruitful experimentally to determine the effects produced by a known cause than to discover the causes of an observed effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage notes that experiment is especially powerful for studying effects of causes (by producing them artificially) and that discovering causes of an effect is often enabled by prior knowledge of effects of causes. Bacon's eagerness to find causes directly is criticized as less effective than the indirect experimental route. Practical advice: devise experiments that produce controlled effects to infer causal relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assuming causes must resemble their effects ('like produces like')
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject the presumption that the conditions or causes of a phenomenon must resemble the phenomenon itself; likeness between cause and effect is not necessary and leads to error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives many examples: the Doctrine of Signatures (using physical resemblance of plants to infer medical uses), assuming compound properties must mirror elemental properties, and planetary analogies (Mars' redness implying war). Anti-patterns include concocting remedies because they resemble the disease or assuming particle-level qualities must have the same name/quality as compound properties. Use observation and controlled tests instead of resemblance-based inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate conditions/causes with the phenomenon (precise distinction between effect and its conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful to distinguish between a phenomenon (effect) and the conditions or causes that produce it; do not define the phenomenon to be the very condition on which it depends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Bacon speaking as if 'heat' were the same as the motion that produces the sensation of heat; elder Darwin defining 'idea' as a motion of fibres. Advice: keep conceptual clarity—describe phenomena and their causes distinctly. Anti-pattern: using language that collapses cause and effect into identity, leading to confusion about what is being explained versus what does the explaining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid homogeneity requirement for causality (causality not limited to 'homogeneous' things)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept the a priori doctrine that cause and effect must be 'homogeneous' or have common properties, a principle that has been used to deny mind-matter interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage cites Victor Cousin, Coleridge, Spinoza, Leibnitz as proponents of the idea that causality holds only between homogeneous things, producing philosophical positions like pre-established harmony or occasional causes. Guidance: treat such homogeneity requirements skeptically—interaction between heterogeneous domains (e.g., mind and matter) cannot be ruled out merely by an a priori homogeneity demand.
